U.S. citizenship · Saipan

Is a Baby Born in Saipan a U.S. Citizen?

Generally, yes.

A baby born in Saipan (Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands) on or after November 4, 1986 generally acquires U.S. citizenship at birth under Section 303 of the CNMI Covenant. Exceptions and changes in the law may affect individual cases. A child’s citizenship does not grant either parent a visa, green card or permission to enter the United States.

Legal update (June 30, 2026): the U.S. Supreme Court rejected the federal executive order restricting birthright citizenship in Trump v. Barbara. Saipan also has a specific statutory rule under Section 303 of the CNMI Covenant. Confirm unusual diplomatic or individual circumstances with official agencies and a qualified lawyer.

The four decisions to separate

Baby’s nationality

Generally U.S. citizenship at birth; a narrow exception applies to children of certain accredited diplomats.

Parents’ admission

An approved visa or travel authorization does not guarantee entry; CBP decides at the border.

Birth-tourism rule

A visitor visa cannot be issued when the primary purpose is giving birth to obtain U.S. citizenship for the child.

Baby’s travel documents

Certified birth record and U.S. passport are separate applications; return-entry rules depend on the destination.

Why Saipan birth counts

The U.S. Department of State says that people born in the CNMI after November 3, 1986 acquire citizenship at birth under Covenant Section 303. It also requires appropriate evidence of birth. Foreign-diplomat exceptions and any later legal changes should be checked individually. Department of State ↗

Can international parents enter Saipan to give birth?

Pregnancy is not itself a blanket ban on entry. However, CBP considers due date, planned stay, medical coverage, ability to pay and intention to depart. Be truthful about your purpose of travel. Medical treatment and birth tourism are not interchangeable visa purposes.

Visitor visa rules ↗ · CBP guidance ↗

Documents after birth

1 · Record the birth

Ask the delivering hospital and CNMI vital-records office how to obtain a certified birth certificate; verify all names and spellings.

2 · Apply for the child’s U.S. passport

Check the U.S. Department of State’s under-16 instructions for DS-11, evidence of citizenship, parental relationship, identity, consent and in-person attendance.

3 · Confirm onward or return travel

Ask your country’s consulate and airline which nationality and entry documents apply to your baby. A U.S. passport alone may not resolve every destination-country question.

Official under-16 passport instructions ↗

Before booking travel

  • Get written confirmation that a maternity provider can accept the pregnancy and provide emergency and newborn care.
  • Request an itemized quotation including prenatal visits, delivery, emergency care and possible neonatal intensive care. No price or outcome is guaranteed.
  • Discuss travel timing and flying risks with your obstetric clinician and airline.
  • Confirm entry status, financial documents and passport timing before making nonrefundable bookings.

Frequently asked questions

Do foreign parents have to be U.S. citizens?

No, parental citizenship is generally not a requirement for birth in Saipan under the CNMI rule, but diplomatic exceptions and changes in law may matter.

Do the parents automatically get green cards?

No. A U.S. citizen generally must be at least 21 to petition for a parent, and approval is not automatic.

Does the birth certificate equal a passport?

No. A certified birth certificate can be primary evidence of citizenship, but a passport requires a separate application and review.

Can we enter with a visitor visa mainly to give birth for citizenship?

No. The Department of State expressly identifies that purpose as impermissible for issuance of a visitor visa.

Can the baby also hold the parents’ nationality?

That depends on the relevant country’s nationality law, parental status and documentation rules. Verify with the relevant consular authority.
